title: Guru Arjan: sweetness
hook: the fifth Guru's light: the Lord's will is sweet
tomorrow: why would a Guru strap on two swords?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Ram Das: devotion, a morning kept beside the pool. Today is graduation, and one seat is empty.

Caps, gowns, and a stadium full of phones held high. Simran crosses the stage and her family screams her name, all but one voice. Bebe's knee gave out this week, and the heat was too much, so she's watching on a phone at home. Simran is upset all afternoon, until Bebe calls and says the short line she says whenever a plan breaks: tera bhana meetha. Your will is sweet. How can anyone call a hard will sweet? This one is a hard story, told gently.
screen: `CAPS, GOWNS, PHONES HELD HIGH.` → `ONE SEAT EMPTY.` → `TERA BHANA MEETHA.`

segments.voice: The line comes from Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in Raag Asa, Ang 394. In paraphrase: what you do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. Tradition remembers that Guru Arjan, who gathered the Gurus' hymns into one book, was tortured in Lahore and died there, holding to this sweetness through it. Sweet doesn't mean pain is nice. It means the will isn't his enemy. Something to tell a friend tonight: Sikhs remember a Guru who died under torture by a line about sweetness. Now the week, carried back. Your hukam: the day's order, walked in. Your Ardas: remember, then ask, then the good of all. Guru Nanak: wonder, the sky as the platter. Guru Angad: humility, the unseen pots. Guru Amar Das: equality, one clay in one row. Guru Ram Das: devotion, a morning kept. And today, sweetness: the plan breaks, and you still say the line. Bebe, on the phone, asks to see the diploma up close, and holds the screen to her forehead.
screen: `WHAT YOU DO SEEMS SWEET.` · `SWEET DOESN'T MEAN PAINLESS.` · `A WEEK OF LIGHTS, CARRIED BACK.` · `THE PLAN BREAKS; SAY THE LINE.` · then, large: `SWEET WILL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing this week that didn't go your way, small or large. Hold it for a few slow breaths without arguing with it. If you pray, you can say Guru Arjan's words under your breath, tera bhana meetha; if not, let your shoulders drop each time you breathe out.
Guru Arjan: the fifth Guru, whose light is sweetness. What you do seems sweet to me, even on the hard days.
Last line of the week: sweet will, the plan breaks and the line holds. Seven days, five Gurus, one diploma.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan's martyrdom each year, and in the summer heat many gurdwaras and families set up chhabeels, stalls of cold sweetened water, in his memory; 'tera bhana meetha laage' is a line Sikhs say when accepting what comes.

chat.meaning: Guru Arjan calls God's doing sweet, and tradition says he held to it through torture. Sweet means not an enemy, not painless.
